name: Spizzichino
description: Spizzichino (or 'Pizzichino') is a complex two-player Italian card game played with a 40-card deck (Italian suits). It combines elements of Briscola (trick-taking) and Scopa (capture/fishing) with meld-making (similar to Bezique/Pinochle). The name likely refers to 'picking' or 'nibbling' at points in small increments. The game is highly strategic and lesser-known outside Italy.

history.origins: Dates to the 18th or 19th century. A hybrid of Tressette mechanics (ranking 3-2-A) and Scopa capture? No, usually Tressette ranking.
timeline: 1900s: Fades slightly but maintained in Southern Italy.
history.cultural: A game for serious card players who enjoy counting and melding.
history.evolution: The melding mechanics ('Accuse') add layers of strategy.

setup.players: Two players; they take turns to deal. Each player has a hand of 10 cards and two face-up packets of 5 cards on the table (only the top card of each packet is visible). Play is from hand or from the top of a packet.
setup.dealing: Dealer shuffles and creates eight packets of 5 cards face down. Opponent chooses four packets: two placed face-up on the table (top card visible only), two picked up as a 10-card hand. Dealer does the same with the other four. Each player has a 10-card hand and two face-up packets of 5 cards.
setup.equipment: 40-card Italian pack (Latin suits). In some regions a 40-card French pack with Queen replacing Cavallo.

rules.objective: Score more points than your opponent by winning tricks (card points plus last-trick bonus) and declaring buongiochi (three or four of a rank, or Napoletana 3-2-A of a suit). The game ends when a player reaches 51 or more points.
rules.gameplay: Two players play 20 tricks. Non-dealer leads first; winner of each trick leads the next. You may play from your hand or the top of one of your two face-up packets (revealing the next card). Must follow suit when possible. Same suit: higher card wins; different suit: lead wins. Honours (3, 2, Ace) on top of a packet may be moved to hand. Declare buongiochi (three or four of same rank, or Napoletana 3-2-A of a suit) when acquired to score 3 or 4 points. After 20 tricks, count card points in tricks won plus 1 for last trick; add meld points. Game ends when a player reaches 51 points.
keyRules: Same suit: higher card wins; different suit: lead wins.

Game ends when a player reaches 51 points.

strategy.basic: Prioritize melds. A Napola is worth 3 points immediately plus card values. Save your 3s, 2s, and Aces for this purpose. Don't play them on empty tricks if you can meld them.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Pizzico': 'Nibbling' points. If you see your opponent collecting a suit for Napola, lead that suit to break their run or force them to play high.
strategy.advanced: Counting the Tick: There are 10 points and 2/3rds in the deck. Total score is 11 points (plus melds). Knowing exactly how many points have been played is vital for the endgame squeeze.

variations.name: Look at bottom of packets
variations.description: Before choosing which packets to turn up, each player may look at the bottom card of their own packets.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Optional rule only; no engine constants change for this variant.

variations.name: No buongiochi
variations.description: Buongiochi are not declared or scored; game is played to 21 or 31 points instead of 51.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Target score and meld scoring differ; overrides can be added when mapping constants.

variations.name: Tressette in Due a Metà Mazzo
variations.description: Alternative variant: deal 10 each, 20 cards as stock. After each trick both players draw from stock (winner first) and show the card. Declare buongiochi before first trick or when a draw completes a new combination. Game to 21, 31, 41 or 51.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Different deal and draw rules; engine overrides to be added when implementing this variant.

scoring.winCondition: Score points through melds and tricks.
